title: Security Governance Principles
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 1: Security and Risk Management: Security Governance Principles.

items: Security governance must be aligned with corporate governance
Governance = directing the organization to achieve its goals and objectives
CEO is ultimately accountable for organizational governance
Security function should be viewed as an organizational enabler
CISO/CSO reports organizational security posture to executive leadership

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: "Governance means to govern properly to allow the organization to achieve its goals and objectives focused on increasing the value of the organization for the stakeholders." Security governance involves:

items: Aligning the organization's security function to business strategy, goals, mission, and objectives
Defining organizational roles and responsibilities for security
Managing security policies, standards, baselines, guidelines, and procedures
Monitoring compliance with security policies

blocks.text: One way an organization can establish sound governance aligned with security is through the establishment of an Organizational Governance Committee, charged with promoting the top-down governance structure critical to achieving organizational goals. From Destination CISSP: "If the CEO regularly communicates the need for robust security that is aligned with the strategy, goals, mission, and objectives of the organization, the security function will be viewed as a great asset and an organizational enabler." ⚠️ Exam Trap: Security governance is a MANAGEMENT function, not a technical one. The CISSP exam expects you to think about governance from a business perspective.

items: CEO — Ultimately accountable for organizational governance and security
CISO/CSO — Responsible for security program implementation
Board of Directors — Oversight and fiduciary responsibility
Data Owner — Accountable for classification and protection of data
Data Custodian — Day-to-day data management and protection

rows: Ultimate accountability for organizational governance; sets tone from top
Classification decisions; defines access requirements; usually senior management
Day-to-day data handling; backups, restoration; implements controls per Owner's direction
Business responsibility for data quality, metadata, governance, compliance
Processes data on behalf of the Data Controller (GDPR term)
Determines purposes and means of processing personal data (GDPR term)
Individual to whom personal data pertains

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: "Owners are ultimately accountable for an asset and protecting its value. Owners should understand the importance of following governance mandates and the need to classify each asset they're accountable for." ⚠️ Exam Trap: Data Owners are management/executives who make classification decisions. Data Custodians are IT staff who implement the technical controls. Don't confuse these roles.

items: Policies — High-level management directives; compulsory; define "what"
Standards — Compulsory requirements for uniform use of technology
Baselines — Minimum security configuration levels
Guidelines — Recommended actions; not compulsory (advisory)
Procedures — Step-by-step instructions; define "how"

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: "Once policies are set, the remaining security documentation can be crafted under the guidance of those policies. Standards define compulsory requirements for the homogenous use of hardware, software, technology, and security controls." From Stewart: "All too often, policies, standards, baselines, guidelines, and procedures are developed only as an afterthought or in response to a security incident." From Shon Harris: "Guidelines outline methodologies, include suggested actions, and are not compulsory." Guidelines deal with gray areas where specific standards don't apply. Mnemonic: Policies → Standards → Baselines → Guidelines → Procedures (from most strategic to most operational: "People Should Be Good Practitioners") ⚠️ Exam Trap: Guidelines are the ONLY non-mandatory document in the hierarchy. Everything else (policies, standards, baselines, procedures) is compulsory.

items: Data Owner/Controller — Accountable for protection; defines classification and access
Data Custodian — Implements technical controls; day-to-day management
Data Steward — Business responsibility for data quality and governance
Data Processor — Processes data on behalf of the controller (GDPR)
Data Subject — Individual whose personal data is being processed

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: Data Owners are typically senior management who:

items: Define classification levels for their data
Approve access requests
Define retention and destruction requirements
Are ultimately accountable for data protection

blocks.text: From Official CBK (Table 2-3): Different types of owners exist with different responsibilities related to data protection, including defining security requirements, deciding access rights, and assisting in risk assessment. Data Custodians are typically IT staff who:

items: Implement and maintain security controls
Perform regular backups
Manage data storage
Ensure data integrity through technical means

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: The Owner makes the DECISIONS. The Custodian IMPLEMENTS the decisions. If a question asks "who decides classification?" — it's the Owner. If it asks "who performs backups?" — it's the Custodian.

items: Administrative (Managerial) — Policies, procedures, training
Technical (Logical) — Hardware/software controls (firewalls, encryption)
Physical — Locks, fences, guards, environmental controls
Preventive — Stop incidents before they occur
Detective — Identify incidents during or after occurrence
Corrective — Fix problems after detection
Deterrent — Discourage violations
Compensating — Alternative when primary control isn't feasible
Directive — Specify required actions (policies, signs)
Recovery — Restore systems to normal operation

blocks.text: Controls are classified by category (administrative/technical/physical) AND by type (what they do functionally). Any control can be mapped to both dimensions:

From Chapple: "A compensation control provides an alternative when it isn't possible to implement the preferred control." Example: If you can't implement biometric access, you might use smart card + PIN as a compensating control. From Stewart: "Directive access controls include security policy requirements or criteria, posted notifications, escape route exit signs, monitoring, supervision, and procedures." ⚠️ Exam Trap: Don't confuse categories with types. A firewall is a TECHNICAL control (category) that performs a PREVENTIVE function (type). The exam often asks you to classify controls by both dimensions.

items: Due Care — Doing what a reasonable person would do (acting responsibly)
Due Diligence — Research and assessment before making decisions
Both are legal standards that protect against negligence claims
Due Care = "doing the right thing"; Due Diligence = "knowing the right thing"
Failure to exercise due care/diligence may result in legal liability

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: "Prudence implies a proactive and diligent approach to decision-making. In a legal context, acting prudently may serve to protect an individual or organization from liability." Due Care is the action — implementing appropriate security controls, following policies, responding to incidents. It means taking reasonable steps to protect assets. Due Diligence is the investigation — researching threats, understanding risks, evaluating controls before implementing them. It means understanding your environment. Example:

items: Due Diligence = Researching patch management best practices
Due Care = Actually applying patches in a timely manner

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Remember: Due Diligence = "homework" (research/planning). Due Care = "action" (implementation/maintenance). Both are required to avoid negligence.
